paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

The United Netherlands form a confederacy of republics, or rather of aristocracies, with a very remarkable structure. Yet they confirm every lesson we have drawn from the confederacies already reviewed.

The union consists of seven sovereign states, equal in rank, and each state or province is in turn made up of equal and independent cities. On every important question, not only the provinces but the cities as well must be unanimous.

The States-General represent the sovereignty of the Union. They usually number about fifty deputies, appointed by the provinces. Their terms differ: some deputies sit for life, others for six years, three years, or one, and two provinces keep their deputies in office only during pleasure.

The States-General may enter into treaties and alliances, make war and peace, raise armies and equip fleets, fix quotas, and demand contributions. In all these matters, however, they need unanimity and the approval of those they represent. They may also appoint and receive ambassadors, carry out treaties and alliances already made, arrange for the collection of duties on imports and exports, regulate the mint (subject to the rights of the provinces), and govern the dependent territories as sovereigns. The provinces may not, without general consent, make foreign treaties, set up imposts that harm other provinces, or charge their neighbors higher duties than they charge their own subjects. A council of state, a chamber of accounts, and five colleges of admiralty support and strengthen the federal administration.

The union's chief executive is the stadtholder, who is now a hereditary prince. His main weight and influence in the republic rest on several things: this independent title; his large inherited estates; his family ties with some of the chief potentates of Europe; and, more than all of these, perhaps, the fact that he is stadtholder in the individual provinces as well as for the union. In that provincial role he appoints town officials under certain regulations, carries out provincial decrees, presides in the provincial courts whenever he chooses, and holds the power of pardon in every province.
Even as stadtholder of the union, though, he has considerable prerogatives.

In his political capacity he may settle disputes between the provinces when other methods fail, attend the deliberations of the States-General and their special conferences, receive foreign ambassadors, and maintain agents for his own affairs at foreign courts.

In his military capacity he commands the federal troops, provides for garrisons, and generally manages military affairs. He makes every appointment from colonel down to ensign, and fills the governorships and posts of fortified towns.

In his naval capacity he is admiral-general. He oversees and directs everything that concerns the naval forces and other naval affairs, presides over the admiralties in person or through a deputy, appoints lieutenant-admirals and other officers, and sets up councils of war, whose sentences are not carried out until he approves them.
His revenue, apart from his private income, comes to three hundred thousand florins. The standing army under his command numbers about forty thousand men.

That is the celebrated Belgic confederacy as it is set down on parchment. What features has practice stamped upon it? A feeble government; discord among the provinces; foreign influence and indignities; an uncertain existence in peace, and special calamities in war.
Grotius observed long ago that only his countrymen's hatred of the house of Austria saved them from being ruined by the vices of their constitution.

Another respected writer says that the union of Utrecht places in the States-General an authority that seems enough to ensure harmony, but that the jealousy in each province makes the practice very different from the theory.

Another says that the same instrument requires each province to levy certain contributions, but that this article never could be carried out and probably never will be, because the inland provinces, having little commerce, cannot pay an equal quota.

On contributions, the usual practice is to set the articles of the constitution aside. The danger of delay forces the consenting provinces to supply their quotas without waiting for the rest, and then to recover the money from the others through deputations, which are frequent, or by whatever other means they can. The great wealth and influence of the province of Holland let her achieve both ends.

More than once the deficiencies have finally had to be collected at the point of the bayonet. That can be done, though it is dreadful, in a confederacy where one member exceeds all the others in strength and several are too small to think of resisting. It is utterly impossible in a confederacy whose members include several that are equal to each other in strength and resources, and each equal by itself to a vigorous and lasting defense.

Sir William Temple, who was himself a foreign minister, says that foreign ministers get around matters taken ad referendum by tampering with the provinces and cities. In 1726 the treaty of Hanover was held up in this way for a whole year. Instances of the same kind are numerous and notorious.

In critical emergencies the States-General are often forced to go beyond their constitutional limits. In 1688 they concluded a treaty on their own authority, at the risk of their heads. The treaty of Westphalia, in 1648, which formally and finally recognized their independence, was concluded without the consent of Zealand. Even in the recent treaty of peace with Great Britain, the constitutional principle of unanimity was set aside. A weak constitution must end one of two ways: in dissolution, for want of proper powers, or in the usurpation of the powers needed for the public safety. Whether the usurpation, once begun, will stop at the beneficial point or go on to the dangerous extreme depends on the chance events of the moment. Tyranny has perhaps more often grown out of assumptions of power that a defective constitution made necessary in pressing emergencies than out of the full exercise of the greatest constitutional authorities.

Calamities have come from the stadtholdership, and yet it has been supposed that without his influence in the individual provinces, the causes of anarchy so plain in the confederacy would long ago have dissolved it. "Under such a government," says the Abbe Mably, "the Union could never have subsisted, if the provinces had not a spring within themselves, capable of quickening their tardiness, and compelling them to the same way of thinking. This spring is the stadtholder." Sir William Temple observes "that in the intermissions of the stadtholdership, Holland, by her riches and her authority, which drew the others into a sort of dependence, supplied the place."

Other circumstances, too, have held back the tendency to anarchy and dissolution. The surrounding powers make union to a certain degree an absolute necessity, and at the same time their intrigues feed the constitutional vices that keep the republic, to some degree, always at their mercy.

True patriots have long grieved over the fatal tendency of these vices. They have made no fewer than four regular attempts to find a remedy, by means of EXTRAORDINARY ASSEMBLIES called together for that special purpose. Each time their praiseworthy zeal has found it impossible to UNITE THE PUBLIC COUNCILS in reforming the known, the acknowledged, the fatal evils of the existing constitution. Let us pause for a moment, my fellow-citizens, over this sad and cautionary lesson of history. With the tear we shed for the calamities that conflicting opinions and selfish passions have brought on mankind, let us join a prayer of thanks to Heaven for the fortunate harmony that has marked the consultations about our political happiness.
A plan was also conceived to set up a general tax to be administered by the federal authority. This too had its opponents and failed.

This unhappy people now appear to be in the crisis of their destiny, suffering from popular convulsions, from dissensions among the states, and from actual invasion by foreign arms. All nations have their eyes fixed on this awful spectacle. The first wish that humanity prompts is that this severe trial may result in such a revolution in their government as will establish their union and make it the parent of tranquillity, freedom and happiness. The next is that the asylum in which, we trust, these blessings will soon be secured in this country may receive them and console them for the catastrophe of their own.

I offer no apology for having dwelt so long on these federal precedents. Experience is the oracle of truth, and when its answers are unambiguous, they ought to be conclusive and sacred. The important truth that it declares without ambiguity in the present case is this: a sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities as opposed to individuals, is a solecism in theory, and in practice it destroys the order and ends of civil government. It puts VIOLENCE in the place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in the place of the mild and beneficial COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.
